title: Half-Wave Rectifier: How a Diode Turns AC into Pulses
topic: Half-wave rectifier — a diode in series with a load conducts on positive half-cycles and blocks on negative, turning an AC sinusoid into a one-sided pulse train

beats.narration: An AC source plus a diode — what shape comes out across the load?

elements.content: AC in — what waveform comes out the other side?

beats.narration: Put a diode in series with a resistor. The diode passes current one way, blocks it the other.

elements.content: AC source symbol on the left (sine inside a circle)
Diode in series — triangle + bar with arrow pointing right (anode → cathode)
Resistor (load) on the right of the diode
Return wire closing the loop along the bottom
V_in label on the source, V_out label across the resistor
current can only flow one way — anode → cathode

beats.narration: When V in goes positive, the diode is forward biased and current flows. When V in swings negative, the diode reverse biases and the current stops.

elements.content: Two-panel split: 'forward bias' on the left (diode bright, current arrow flowing through load)
'reverse bias' on the right (diode dim with X, no current arrow)
ON when V_in > 0  ·  OFF when V_in < 0

beats.narration: Watch V in trace as a smooth sinusoid, while V out keeps only the positive humps — the negative half is clipped to zero.

elements.content: Two stacked scope panels — V_in on top, V_out below; shared time axis
V_in: a smooth sinusoid drawn left-to-right via TraceIn over the scope window
V_out: clipped sinusoid (positive humps only, flat zero on negative half) drawn synchronously with V_in
elements.note: the genuine motion of this scene

elements.content: Live diode-state badge that toggles between 'ON' (amber) and 'OFF' (rose) as the cursor crosses each half-cycle
the negative half is cut to zero

beats.narration: That's half wave rectification — a single diode turning AC into a pulsing one-sided signal.

elements.content: one diode is the first step of every DC power supply
smoothing comes next — add a capacitor and you get nearly DC
